item.title: AM 015. Weather forecasting: Richardson's failure, Lorenz's wall, and the machines
item.description:
Numerical weather prediction as an initial value problem: why Richardson's hand forecast blew up, the Courant Friedrichs Lewy cost of resolution, Lorenz chaos and the two-week limit, data assimilation as GPS-style least squares, ensembles, and what machine learning models did and did not change.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. Richardson's method was essentially correct, yet his six-hour forecast predicted a wildly unrealistic pressure change. What went wrong with his initial state, and why did a small error in the observed winds produce such a large error in the pressure tendency? 2. Why does halving the grid spacing of a weather model cost far more than twice the computing power? What role does the Courant Friedrichs Lewy condition play? 3. Why is the forecast-length gain from better initial measurements logarithmic rather than proportional, and why does Lorenz's multi-scale argument say even perfect measurement would not push the horizon out indefinitely? 4. In data assimilation, how can a single wind observation over the ocean improve the estimate of the pressure field there, which was never measured? Connect it to how a GPS receiver handles its clock error. 5. Why does a deterministic neural forecast trained on average squared error get blurrier at long lead times even while its scores stay good, and how do ensemble or probabilistic approaches address it?

item.title: PM 014. Robert Moses: how one unelected man ran a city for forty years
item.description:
How Robert Moses built durable power without votes: bill drafting, public authorities that compounded toll revenue into new bonds, covenants shielded by the contract clause, and the threat to resign. Then the costs, the tangled low-bridge story, his fall through Rockefeller and Chase Manhattan, and the three faces of power.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. The original idea of a public authority was that it would pay off its bonds and wind down. Explain how Moses turned Triborough into something that grew instead, and why that growth made him harder to remove. 2. Why could a bond covenant protect a public official from an elected legislature? What role does the contract clause play, and why did it matter that new bonds kept being issued? 3. Why was the identity of the bondholders' trustee so important to Rockefeller's ability to merge Triborough into the MTA? 4. Robert Dahl studied the decisions that got fought over and concluded power was spread out. Using the second face of power, explain what a study like that would have missed about Moses. 5. The low-bridge story is often told as simple deliberate exclusion. What does the careful version say is well established, what remains uncertain, and why?

item.title: AM 013. Haber-Bosch: how a catalyst pulls bread out of the air
item.description:
Why dinitrogen is so inert, the thermodynamics-versus-kinetics trap in ammonia synthesis, what the iron surface and its promoters actually do, the Sabatier principle and volcano plots, how Bosch industrialized Haber's lab result, and how nitrogenase does it at room temperature.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. A catalyst can't change the equilibrium yield of ammonia. So why does a better catalyst still increase how much ammonia you get from each pass through the reactor? 2. Why does raising the pressure help the ammonia yield while raising the temperature hurts it, even though both make molecules collide more often? 3. By the Sabatier principle, why would a metal that binds nitrogen atoms much more strongly than iron be a worse catalyst, even though it splits nitrogen more easily? 4. In Bosch's reactor, what did hot hydrogen do to ordinary steel, and why did a low-carbon inner liner with a vented outer shell solve it? 5. Nitrogenase works at room temperature, so why isn't it simply more efficient than the industrial process? What does it spend instead of heat, and where is the waste?

item.title: PM 012. The science of cooking: why recipes say what they say
item.description:
Heat as diffusion (time scales with thickness squared), the Maillard reaction and the searing myth, protein denaturation in eggs and meat, how salt and brining really work, emulsions and why mayonnaise is stiff, gluten, leavening and why bread stales in the fridge, and what Salt Lake's altitude does to all of it.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. A recipe says a two inch roast needs about twice as long as a one inch roast. Using how heat diffuses into food, explain why that estimate is wrong, and why a very hot oven makes the overcooked outer band worse. 2. Why does a wet or crowded surface prevent browning even in a very hot pan, and if searing doesn't seal in juices, what is the actual reason to sear? 3. Steak and brisket are both beef. In terms of muscle fiber proteins and collagen, why should one be cooked fast and stopped early while the other needs hours, and why is a brisket pulled at a normal 'done' temperature tough? 4. Why does mayonnaise end up thick and spoonable when it's made of oil and a watery liquid, and why must the first oil go in drop by drop? 5. Bread goes stale after a day in the fridge but weighs almost the same. What happened inside it, why did the fridge speed that up, and why does warming it in the oven temporarily help?

item.title: AM 011. Error-correcting codes: from Shannon's limit to your phone
item.description:
Shannon's noisy channel theorem and why capacity is a cliff, Hamming's self-locating parity checks, Reed-Solomon polynomials and why erasures cost half what errors do, then turbo codes, Gallager's rediscovered LDPC codes and polar codes in 5G, ending with quantum error correction. Opens with a callback on GPS's eccentricity correction.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. Repetition codes can drive the error rate down, so what exactly did Shannon's theorem claim that repetition cannot do, and why does his random coding argument not hand engineers a usable code? 2. In the seven-four Hamming code, why do three parity checks suffice to locate a single error among seven bits, and what property of the way the checks are assigned makes the syndrome equal to the error's position? 3. A Reed-Solomon code with a given number of redundant symbols can fix twice as many erasures as errors. Explain why, in terms of unknowns and equations, and explain how interleaving plus erasure flagging lets a CD survive a long scratch. 4. Why does soft decision decoding beat hard decision decoding, and in an LDPC decoder, why does the parity-check graph need to be sparse for belief propagation to work well? 5. Quantum mechanics forbids copying an unknown state and disturbs a qubit when you measure it. How does quantum error correction get around both problems, and what is the significance of operating below the error threshold?

item.title: PM 010. The shipping container: how a steel box rewired the world economy
item.description:
Why the container only paid off once institutions changed around it: ICC regulation that kept transport modes apart, the committee fight over box sizes and corner fittings, the longshore deals that traded work rules for a share of the gains, port authorities and the Vietnam War, and what the evidence says about its effect on trade and supply-chain fragility.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. In the break bulk era, why was the cost of trade concentrated in port rather than at sea, and what exactly did the container eliminate? 2. Why did the Interstate Commerce Commission's way of regulating transport make the container hard to exploit, and why did McLean have to give up control of his trucking company? 3. Why did the pioneers, Sea-Land with 35-foot boxes and Matson with 24-foot boxes, end up outside the standard sizes, and why would McLean's company release its corner-fitting patents for free? 4. What did West Coast longshoremen give up and get in the 1960 Mechanization and Modernization Agreement, and what is the main criticism of that kind of deal? 5. Why did containerization concentrate shipping in a few giant hub ports rather than spreading it out, and how does that connect to the supply-chain fragility seen during the pandemic?

item.title: AM 009. The end of Dennard scaling: why clock speeds stopped rising
item.description:
Why Moore's law (transistor counts) outlived Dennard scaling (constant power density): the constant-field arithmetic, the sixty-millivolt-per-decade Boltzmann limit and gate tunneling that froze voltage, the fixes from high-k metal gates to FinFETs and gate-all-around, and how multicore, dark silicon and specialized accelerators followed.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. Under Dennard's constant-field scaling, walk through why power density stays constant. Which term in the dynamic power equation does the heavy lifting, and what happens to power density if voltage is held fixed while everything else scales? 2. Why does the sixty millivolts per factor of ten limit not improve as transistors get smaller, and why does that limit put a floor under the supply voltage? 3. High-k dielectrics let the gate insulator get physically thicker. Explain why a thicker layer helps with one problem while preserving performance, and name the leakage problem it does not solve. 4. What problem does wrapping the gate around more of the channel solve, first with fins and then with nanosheets? Explain the mechanism in terms of who controls the barrier in the channel. 5. Why can two cores at lower voltage and frequency deliver more throughput than one fast core for the same power, and why did dark silicon push design toward specialized accelerators rather than simply more general-purpose cores?

item.title: PM 008. Milgram and the Stanford Prison Experiment: what they showed, and what they didn't
item.description:
Milgram's obedience studies and their two dozen variations, what the Yale archives revealed (improvised prods, partial disbelief, a direct order that failed), why the Stanford Prison Experiment's famous conclusion collapsed, the BBC Prison Study and truncated replications, and engaged followership as the rival theory.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. Across Milgram's variations, obedience ranged from nearly everyone to nearly no one. Pick three of the variations and explain what each one changed, and what that pattern tells you that a single headline number cannot. 2. Perry and colleagues found that participants who believed the learner was really in pain were more likely to defy the experimenter. Explain why that finding pushes the headline obedience rate in a particular direction, and why a post-experiment questionnaire is still weak evidence on its own. 3. The fourth prod, 'you have no other choice, you must go on', was the only direct order in Milgram's script, and it was the least effective. Why is that a problem for the agentic state theory, and how does engaged followership explain it? 4. Explain why the Stanford Prison Experiment, as run, could not support its famous conclusion that roles spontaneously turn ordinary people cruel. Name both a design flaw and something specific the archives revealed. 5. In the BBC Prison Study, tyranny eventually became a live possibility, but not the way Stanford suggested. What was the mechanism there, and how does it differ from the claim that a role by itself corrupts the person who plays it?

item.title: AM 007. How CRISPR finds one sequence among three billion
item.description:
CRISPR as a bacterial immune system, and the search problem at its core: how Cas9 finds one twenty-letter address in a three-billion-letter genome. The PAM handshake as a cheap reject, the directional R-loop zipper and why seed mismatches matter more, kinetic proofreading via the conformational gate, and why repair pathways (not the cut) decide what you can actually edit. Opens with a callback on GPS clock bias and the dual-frequency ionosphere trick.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. Checking for the three-letter handshake only narrows the candidate sites by a factor of about eight, leaving hundreds of millions of positions in the human genome. Explain why this still makes the search tractable. What is the expensive operation that the handshake check protects, and why can the handshake be read without performing it? 2. Cas9 is much less tolerant of mismatches near the handshake than of mismatches at the far end of the twenty-letter target, even though all twenty positions are logically equivalent as information. Explain the mechanism that creates this asymmetry. 3. Why is it important that the conformational change licensing the cut happens only after the full-length match forms, rather than the protein cutting as soon as it is stably bound? Frame your answer in terms of what would go wrong with near-matches under the second design. 4. High-fidelity Cas9 variants are made by weakening the protein's non-specific contacts with the DNA backbone, not by changing the guide RNA. Explain why weakening a non-specific grip improves sequence specificity, and what you give up in exchange. 5. The sickle cell therapy does not correct the sickle cell mutation. It breaks a regulatory element so that fetal hemoglobin is produced instead. Explain why that indirect approach was easier, in terms of the two DNA repair pathways and which cells they work in.

item.title: PM 006. Why chord progressions work: the guitar as a system
item.description:
Harmonics and roughness (and the Tsimane study on how much consonance preference is learned), the Pythagorean comma and equal temperament, the fretboard as a lattice, Roman-numeral chords, the tritone engine of the five-seven resolution, and why rock's grammar breaks the classical rules.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. Why do intervals with simple frequency ratios, like the octave and the fifth, tend to sound smoother than intervals with complicated ratios? Explain the mechanism in terms of harmonics, then explain why the Tsimane study means this mechanism alone doesn't explain why people enjoy resolution. 2. Why can't any tuning system make every fifth and every octave perfectly pure at the same time? What does equal temperament give up, and what does it gain, by dividing the octave into twelve identical ratios? 3. On a guitar, why can you slide a chord shape up the neck and get the same type of chord in a new key? And why does a shape need adjusting when it crosses from the G string to the B string? 4. Why does the five seven chord pull so strongly to the one chord? Which two notes do the work, what interval do they form, and where does each one move? 5. Rock progressions often use the flat seven chord in a major key. What does lowering that seventh scale degree remove from the harmony, and why might that make a resolution sound blunter or more settled rather than urgent?

item.title: AM 005. How the grid holds 60 hertz, and how Texas nearly lost it
item.description:
Frequency as the grid's real-time supply-demand ledger, inertia and the swing equation, governor droop and automatic generation control, under-frequency load shedding, what actually failed in Texas in February 2021, and how inverter-based grids replace inertia on purpose.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. Why does grid frequency drop when load exceeds generation? Where does the missing energy come from in the first few seconds, and why does that make frequency a system-wide signal of the supply and demand balance? 2. Using the swing equation, why does replacing half of a grid's synchronous generation with solar and batteries make the same plant trip more dangerous, even with unchanged total capacity? Which part of the frequency response does it affect, and why? 3. Why do governors use droop rather than every generator trying to hold exactly 60 hertz? What problem does droop solve, and what does it leave unsolved that automatic generation control fixes? 4. Why is deliberately cutting power to customers the protective response when frequency falls too far? Describe the feedback loop load shedding interrupts, including how low frequency attacks a thermal plant's ability to keep running. 5. In Texas in 2021, how did the natural gas system and the electric system make each other's failures worse, and why does that interdependence make a cold snap more dangerous than a count of frozen equipment suggests?

item.title: PM 004. Why Bretton Woods collapsed
item.description:
The 1944 design and the Keynes versus White fight over symmetric adjustment, the short convertible era, Triffin's dilemma as a bank run, the 1960s patches (gold pool, capital controls, two-tier market, SDRs), the Nixon shock and Smithsonian, and the competing explanations for the collapse.
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. Explain Triffin's dilemma as a bank run. What plays the role of deposits, what plays the role of the vault, and why does the system becoming more successful make it more fragile? 2. Keynes's plan put pressure on surplus countries as well as deficit countries. Why did the Americans reject that in 1944, and how did the lack of it come back to hurt the system in the late sixties? 3. Using the trilemma, explain why the growth of the eurodollar market made the fixed pegs harder to hold, and why a doubted peg becomes a one-way bet for speculators. 4. Why did the collapse of the London Gold Pool in 1968, and the two-tier market that replaced it, amount to a major retreat even though the official price stayed at $35? 5. Under a fixed exchange rate system anchored on the dollar, how did rising American inflation in the late sixties get transmitted to countries like Germany, and why did that give them a reason to stop holding dollars?

item.title: AM 003. Gödel's incompleteness theorems: what they actually say
item.description:
Opens with a callback on GPS clock bias. Hilbert's program, Gödel numbering and the diagonal lemma, both incompleteness theorems, the halting-problem route via Turing, and what the theorems don't say (nonstandard models, Presburger arithmetic, Gentzen, Lucas-Penrose).
Quiz (reply in that episode's Daily Lecture chat): 1. If the system is consistent, why must the Gödel sentence be true in the ordinary natural numbers, and why isn't it a contradiction that we can see it is true while the system can't prove it? 2.
